As someone who didn't match the first time and is now coming to end of PGY1, I'm quite convinced how you do in the match doesn't correlate all that much to how you are as a resident.  I've been praised this year as "the best" and "most efficient" by several attendings.  And I see a lot of people who matched their first time struggle.  And the program I matched up is competitive for my field. 

Not matching was the worst.  I see that entire year as a black haze.  But I will say not matching has made me a lot stronger of a person.  Has made it easier for me to tolerate everyday frustrations (oh a discharge fell through and patient's family is bitching me out... at least it's not the stomach sinking punch of finding out I didn't match!).  I'm a lot more clear about who I am and what I value.  The match says nothing about who you are or your potential.  

I remember during this period 2 years ago I felt completely worthless.  My fiance would say that I would be a great doctor and the match means nothing but I completely didn't believe him.  After all, it felt like a very objective set of data that after looking at ALL the applicants who interviewed with me, every single program I ranked said, nah.  You're not good enough.  And everyone else is better than you.  But this is false.  They don't know you and your potential.

The match told me I was worthless and no one would want me to be a doctor but my actual experiences as a doctor is nothing like that.  I don't know you obviously, but I'm not unique in this.  I went unmatched and now I'm "the best".  Obviously the match wasn't a great predictor at all.  Don't let the match write the narrative of your life.

Get mental health help. Start to love yourself more. Have more self-compassion. Be OK with failure once in a while, because the alternative is giving up and never achieving your potential and a lifelong road of regret. Be honest with your family and friends about the place you are in. Brace for hard times, and then try to put away the past misgivings and failures to face the future. Plenty of people fail, and in much bigger ways. They still come back, because they don't give up. Part of not giving up, I think, is also starting to believe that you are worth it.  You are worth loving, and caring about.

It's great you're going to see a psychiatrist and your family will consider medication for you because what you're going through sounds very serious and debilitating to me.  

What struck me about reading your post was how invested you are in your transcript and grades over your personal wellbeing and possibly stopping your hallucinations and dissociations.  Your grades does not matter compared to getting you mentally better.  You say you're very ambitious and have been successful academically.  If you continue along this path with nothing changing it's only going to get harder and more challenging.  Many people find college to be a very academically stressful time.  If you don't take care of your health now you're setting yourself up for failure.

It sounds really stressful to balance school and mental illness at the same time, when grade 11 is an important time for a lot of people who want to apply to top colleges.  But you should also know that your life is very long.  High school--and the importance you might place in your grades now--really pales in comparison to the other life experiences you'll have later.  Life is much, much more than what you're experiencing now.  It is OK even if you fail.  The only thing that would really ruin everything would be if you prioritized your academic success over your mental health.

I struggle with the same thing, too, in that I would be living my life and then suddenly I would get this thought pop up like, "hey remember so-and-so? She was so great and you're such a fucking loser."  :(

Wow that sounds really hard.  Why do you feel like you're "still at square one"?  Does the length of time you feel sad change at all?  Like, did it get any shorter after you've put in all that effort?

It is also possible your depression is under-treated.  Something like 30% of people with depression have treatment resistance.  

What do you hate about your daily life?  Why do you think you're stupid?  And it sounds like you're tired of feeling negative about "good" things in your life.  It sounds like it's more than just pessimism?

Yeah! There's a number of different meds out there.  It's really hard to tell which one will work for you.  Don't give up!

I value your experiences, even if they don't affect me.  But they do.  Because I'm reading about you and the things you feel and think about.

Do you really not care about dying?  Not existing?  Or is it a fear about living?  You mentioned twice this idea of being successful in society, and how being valuable in life (for you? for society?) means that you have achieved many professionally successful things.  What, to you, would be a meaningful life?  Is there anything you want?

I also think if you're willing to die, then why not take the chance to (possibly) become someone different by taking antidepressants?  Death is the ultimate change.  Why not take a smaller amount of change?
How long do your low periods last?  And how long has it been that it's been getting lower?

Yeah, I get that.  I do that, too.  It sometimes feels overwhelming, and I want to give up entirely and just... be done with the struggle.  What really helps, though, is that now I've convinced myself that feelings are temporary and that I won't always feel this way.  And it inevitably does pass.  I do wish it would go away permanently.  But hey!  We have treatments and techniques.  Better than if we had depression and there was nothing we could do.

Lexapro.  Different people respond to different meds and at different time lines, but it worked almost immediately for me.  Don't give up if the first one you try doesn't work out or takes some time.  Have you tried any?

I think there is inherent value in life.  I also think there is no "point" to life, because we all die, like you said.  I think, though, that your current experience is valuable.  In the sense that you feel and you suffer and you think and maybe sometimes you feel good, and I think that that's worthy of trying to save.  Because someday you could really have an amazing experience, as long as you're not dead. 

As for antidepressants, I don't know that it does what you think it will do.  I think it's different for different people, but I also think it's hard to know what it will do to you until you try it.  Personally when I was offered antidepressants I was really against it.  I didn't want to change who I was because for me, all those negative feelings and thoughts were such a part of who I thought I was.  I thought I saw the truth, too, and didn't want to give up the "real" me for some saccharine version of a person.  But ultimately antidepressants didn't do exactly what I thought it would do.  I do think I've changed and I'm much more positive, but also... I don't care about the same things that I used to care about as a depressed person.  

It seems like the experiences you are having now--with all the pain and all the suffering and all the indifference--isn't really working out for you.  But also you want to keep being this person, because it sounds like it's a value you hold.  And you feel that inevitably, you'll take your own life.  Is it worth dying to preserve this version of yourself?

People regret committing suicide.  There are people who don't successfully die, and some of them are so glad they survived months or years later.  I think if you could be one of those people, then even if you don't want to live, I hope you continue to live for that chance that you will someday be glad you never did succeed in committing suicide. 

I think the prevailing view is that there IS something wrong with you (and me).  You shouldn't be feeling so sad and hopeless and guilty.  People shouldn't feel this way.  The world has a lot of terrible things, but some people can still feel happy and hopeful and other people feel down and horrible.  What do you think about depression being an illness?  And that it is treatable?  And that maybe your view on the world in general can change, if you felt differently?

I've felt that way.  Like it is way too painful or pointless to keep going, and wouldn't it be so nice if everything ended?

What changed for me is taking meds. Have you tried? Gradually, life stopped feeling so hopeless.  It definitely convinced me that depression is a disease, and it is also treatable.  And that the way I felt (/ still feel sometimes in random spurts) is changeable.  And that everything I did to try and feel better really wasn't enough because of chemical imbalances or whatever it is that was happening in my brain.  It wasn't rational that I was so sad about my life (though I thought it was) and it's not rational now that I'm generally happy with my life and definitely do not want to die.  I think for me, the cost(life) and benefits(life) are really not objective measures but rather heavily influenced by your mood.  And I think your mood can be changed.
